analysis.one_liner: Raises workplace safety penalties, covers government employees, and strengthens OSHA whistleblower protections.
analysis.headline: Introduced April 28, 2026 with 17 Democratic cosponsors and referred to the Senate labor committee, which has taken no action on it.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill rewrites the Occupational Safety and Health Act of 1970. It extends federal workplace-safety coverage to federal, state, and local government workers, who are currently excluded in states without their own approved safety plans. It raises civil fines roughly tenfold for willful and repeated violations, makes knowingly causing a worker's death a crime punishable by up to 10 years in prison with officers and directors personally liable, gives workers who report safety problems much stronger protection from being fired or punished, and gives injured workers and their families rights to follow and participate in the government's investigation of their case.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers in hazardous jobs — construction, manufacturing, meatpacking, warehousing — get tougher penalties against employers who ignore safety rules, faster investigation of deaths and serious incidents, protection from retaliation when they report injuries or refuse dangerous work, and no loss of pay for helping with a safety inspection. State and local government workers get federal OSHA coverage for the first time. Injured workers and families of killed workers get to meet investigators, receive citations, and speak before penalty settlements.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers in dangerous and public-sector jobs

how_it_helps.text: Extends OSHA coverage to employees of the United States, states, and political subdivisions, closing a gap that leaves government workers outside federal safety enforcement in states without approved plans [S2].

Raises the maximum fine for a willful or repeated violation from $70,000 to $700,000, sets a $30,000 maximum (with a $10,000 minimum) for serious violations, and allows up to $70,000 per day for uncorrected violations, with annual inflation adjustments [S2].

Makes a knowing safety violation that kills a worker a federal crime punishable by up to 10 years in prison (20 for repeat offenders), and adds up to 5 years for knowingly causing serious bodily harm, with officers and directors personally liable [S2].

Strengthens whistleblower rights: a 180-day filing window measured from when the worker knew of the retaliation, preliminary reinstatement orders, compensatory damages, attorney's fees, and a bar on waiving these rights through pre-dispute arbitration or collective bargaining agreements [S2].

Requires employers to promptly report deaths, hospitalizations, amputations, and eye losses; bans policies that discourage injury reporting; and requires public, searchable electronic reporting of injury data [S2].

Gives victims and families the right to meet with investigators, receive citations at the same time as the employer, and be heard before any settlement that reduces a citation, with a designated family liaison at each OSHA area office [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Employers bear higher fines, daily penalties for uncorrected hazards, and new criminal exposure for executives. State and local governments pay to bring government workplaces under safety standards and to amend their own plans within 12 to 24 months where they run programs. Staffing agencies and site-controlling employers must track and report injuries for all workers on a site, including contractors.

drawbacks.text: Penalty increases of roughly tenfold, plus fines of up to $70,000 per day for uncorrected violations, raise operating costs for employers, with the heaviest burden on smaller firms that lack compliance staff [S2].

The criminal provisions make individual officers and directors personally liable, with prison terms of up to 10 years for a knowing violation that causes a worker's death — an exposure critics of such laws argue can punish management choices made in good faith when a hazard's severity was not clear [S2].
Covering state and local government workplaces shifts compliance costs onto public budgets, and states with their own plans must amend them within a year or face federal concurrent enforcement [S2].

The bill lets the federal Labor Secretary reassert direct enforcement in state-plan states it finds deficient, which states that run their own programs view as overriding their authority and creating duplicate enforcement [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The protections aim at a real and measurable harm — workers killed or injured on the job and then unable to contest weak penalties or retaliation. The costs are concentrated and identifiable: higher fines and criminal exposure for employers, and new compliance spending for governments. The bill largely tightens an existing law rather than building a new program, but the tenfold penalty increases and personal criminal liability for executives are aggressive by current standards, and an honest supporter would acknowledge those will draw sustained opposition and litigation.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in late April 2026 and sent to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, where no vote or floor action has been scheduled.

narrative.text: Senator Bernie Sanders introduced the bill on April 28, 2026, joined by 13 original cosponsors [S2].
It was read twice and referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions the same day [S4].
No further action — no committee markup, hearing, or floor vote — appears in the action history [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers keep the current lower OSHA fine schedule and no expanded criminal liability, and state and local government workplaces remain outside federal OSHA coverage in states without approved plans. Supporters hold a live bill but no commitment of committee time.

for.name: Sen. Bernie Sanders
for.role: U.S. Senator from Vermont; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 13 original cosponsors

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and cosponsor is a Democrat or the independent lead sponsor; no Republican has signed on, and Republicans hold 55 Senate seats, so the bill has no stated path to a floor vote.

industries.industry: High-hazard private employers (construction, manufacturing, meatpacking, warehousing)
industries.note: Maximum fines for willful and repeated violations rise from $70,000 to $700,000, serious violations carry a $10,000 minimum, uncorrected hazards can cost $70,000 per day, and knowingly causing a worker's death becomes a crime with officers and directors personally liable. The industry's cost under this bill is precisely the public's gain in enforcement leverage.

Their workplaces become subject to federal OSHA coverage, requiring compliance spending and, in state-plan states, plan amendments within 12 months or potential federal concurrent enforcement. Government employees gain coverage at the same time taxpayers fund the compliance.

The employer with primary control over a multi-employer work site must keep and make available a single injury log covering everyone on the site, including independent contractors — closing a gap where temporary and contract workers' injuries went untracked.

industries.industry: Labor unions and worker safety advocates
industries.note: New 'authorized employee representative' standing, participation rights in inspections, contests, and stay hearings, and no loss of pay for aiding an inspection give unions and worker representatives a formal role in enforcement.

analysis.trajectory: The 119th Congress is still in session, but with no Republican cosponsors and Republicans holding 55 Senate seats, the bill is unlikely to get a committee markup or floor vote and will most likely expire when the Congress ends on January 3, 2027, as most single-party workplace-safety bills do.
